messages.subject: inla.posterior.sample for an rw2 process
parts:
Hello,

I would like to estimate predictions that follow an rw2 process. I understand I can predict the data by simply adding the prediction locations/covariates to the input data with an NA for the dependent variable. However, I would like to learn how to use the inla.posterior.sample(). 

I did search through the list but did not really see a clear example for rw2. If someone would point me in the right direction that would be great. Otherwise, here is, for simplicity, the example from the rw2 documentation:

n = 100
z = seq(0, 6, length.out = n)
y = sin(z) + rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 0.5)
data = data.frame(y = y, z = z)
formula = y ~ f(z, model="rw2")
fit = inla(formula, 
  data=data, 
  family="gaussian", 
  control.compute=list(config=TRUE)
)
ps = inla.posterior.sample(n=100, fit)  # sample from the joint distribution

So I guess my question boils down to, in this case, what is the relationship between the structure matrix ("R") or "Q" (of formulae 1 & 2 in the rw2 document) and the "z:*" (below). That is, how, I do compute the posterior prediction at some new value of "z"? 

Thanks,
Jae

messages.subject: Re: inla.posterior.sample for an rw2 process
parts:
Nevermind. They look to be additive constants for the matching discretized covariates. 

In case anyone else has this question, here is an example:

for a new location of the prediction at new_z = 0.03 which is between

ps = inla.posterior.sample(n=5000, fit)  # sample from the with more realizations to get a better handle on the posteriors

new_z = 0.03
labels = rownames(ps[[1]]$latent)
i = which(labels =="z:0")
j = which(labels =="z:0.0606060606060606")
b = which(labels=="(Intercept)")
summary( sapply( ps, FUN=function(o) {(o$latent[i] +o$latent[j])/2+ o$latent[b]} ) )

  Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
-0.9230 -0.1057  0.0419  0.0421  0.1883  0.8576 

which is close to the deterministic value sin(new_z) = 0.03. 

A linear prediction might not be best but as the discretization seems so fine, might be good enough?

testing at new_z=4.515:
i = which(labels =="z:4.48484848484849")
j = which(labels =="z:4.54545454545455")
b = which(labels=="(Intercept)")
summary( sapply( ps, FUN=function(o) {(o$latent[i] +o$latent[j])/2+ o$latent[b]} ) )
  Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
 -1.498  -1.043  -0.960  -0.961  -0.877  -0.442 

which compares to sin(new_z) = -0.9806

On Thu, 2018-11-22 at 05:39 -0800, Jae Choi wrote:
> Hello,
>
> I would like to estimate predictions that follow an rw2 process. I
> understand I can predict the data by simply adding the prediction
> locations/covariates to the input data with an NA for the dependent
> variable. However, I would like to learn how to use the
> inla.posterior.sample().

Hi,

I saw your reply. it is possible, if you want prediction for a RW2, say, to do this
just using 'values' and not add NA in the data. like this.

r = inla(y ~ -1 + f(idx,model="rw2",constr=FALSE,values=v),
data = list(y = c(1,0,3), idx = c(1,2,3), v = 0:10),
control.family = list(hyper = list(prec = list(initial = 12, fixed=TRUE))))
plot(r$summary.random$idx$mean, ylim = c(-50,50))
lines(r$summary.random$idx$"0.975quant")
lines(r$summary.random$idx$"0.025quant")


--
Håvard Rue

he...@r-inla.org

Ah, ok. Thanks!

The rationale was that sometimes a model might be much more complex and so expensive to compute in terms of time/cpu. Simulations from joint posteriors could help speed up predictions, especially if there are many to do. 

Best regards,
Jae
